📦 Slide 3: Dataset Structure & Merge Logic (Pandas - Jupyter Notebook: DataFrame Operations)
Why Inner Join? Merge Strategy
Inner Join Formulation: Keep only countries present in all source datasets to prevent missing values in regression features.
\( N_{\text{merged}} = N_{\text{Happiness}} \cap N_{\text{Activity}} \cap N_{\text{Economics}} \)
Harmonisation Impact: Standard inner join yields only \(131\) countries. By applying a \(25\)-entry country name alias mapping, we resolved country mismatches (e.g., "United States" vs. "USA") to achieve:
\( N_{\text{harmonized}} = 152 \text{ countries} \)
Resulting Shape: Final dataset matrix of shape \( 152 \times 27 \).
Feature Schema (27 columns)
• Target (1): Happiness Score Avg (10-yr mean 2013–23)
• Socioeconomic (6): GDP per Capita, Health/Life Exp, Family, Freedom, Generosity, Trust
• WHO Inactivity (20): Adults, Adolescents, 70+, by gender (Female/Male)

🔧 Slide 4: Data Cleaning & Imputation Logic (LinearRegression+LogisticRegression: Slide 191)
Outlier Detection & Handling
1. Outlier Detection via IQR (Slide 191): Used to identify extreme data points that could skew linear regression coefficients:
\( \text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 \)
\( \text{Outlier Bounds} = [Q_1 - 1.5 \cdot \text{IQR}, Q_3 + 1.5 \cdot \text{IQR}] \)
where \( Q_1 \) and \( Q_3 \) are the 25th and 75th percentiles of the feature distribution.
2. Imputation Strategy: Missing columns are imputed via Median rather than Mean to protect against outlier bias:
\( x_{\text{imputed}} = \text{median}(X) \)
3. Z-Score Standardisation: Scaled before regression to enable direct coefficient comparison:
\( z_i = \frac{x_i - \mu}{\sigma} \)
Preprocessing Rationale
• Completeness: Zero entries dropped (all 152 rows complete).
• Median Imputation: Robust against skewed distributions which would otherwise pull the mean away from the center.
• Z-Score Scaling: Ensures all features are on a comparable scale, which is a prerequisite for interpreting regression weights.

📊 Slide 6: Understanding Spurious Correlations & Pearson r (Lecture-Seven: Slide 370-376)
Pearson Correlation & Confounding
Pearson Correlation Coefficient (\(r_{xy}\)) (Slide 374):
\( r_{xy} = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_x \sigma_y} \)
Sample Covariance (Slide 370):
\( \text{Cov}(X, Y) = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n - 1} \)
where \( \bar{x}, \bar{y} \) are means and \( \sigma_x, \sigma_y \) are standard deviations.
Spurious Bivariate Correlation: Bivariate analysis yields \( r \approx 0.40 \) between Inactivity and Happiness.
Confounding Pathway
• Confounding Variable (GDP): Wealthy nations have high GDP per capita (linked to happiness, \( r \approx 0.81 \)) and modern sedentary lifestyles (linked to inactivity, \( r \approx 0.58 \)).
• Path diagram: \( \text{Happiness} \leftarrow \text{GDP} \rightarrow \text{Inactivity} \).
• Multivariate Control: OLS Multiple Regression controls for GDP, blocking the backdoor path and collapsing inactivity's coefficient to near zero (\( \beta \approx -0.005, p = 0.938 \)).

🗺️ Slide 7: Feature Selection & Multicollinearity (VIF) (LinearRegression+LogisticRegression: Slide 191)
Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
Auxiliary Regression Equation: Regress predictor \( X_i \) on all other predictors:
\( X_i = \alpha_0 + \sum_{j \neq i} \alpha_j X_j + \varepsilon_i \)
Variance Inflation Factor Formulation (Slide 191):
\( \text{VIF}_i = \frac{1}{1 - R_i^2} \)
where \( R_i^2 \) is the coefficient of determination from the auxiliary regression.
Resolution: Raw "GDP per Capita" (\( \text{VIF} \approx 15.2 \)) is replaced with its natural logarithm "Log GDP" (\( \text{VIF} \approx 3.8 \)), stabilizing OLS coefficients.
Model Stability Metrics
Raw GDP VIF: 15.2 → Log GDP VIF: 3.8 (Stable)
Social Support VIF: 2.9 | Life Expectancy VIF: 3.4
Inactivity VIF: 1.4 (Extremely stable)
Average VIF of final feature set: 2.8

🤖 Slide 8: Feature Importance & Gini Impurity Reduction Math (Lecture-Five: Slide 264 | RF: Slide 318)
Random Forest Feature Importance (Mean Decrease in Impurity - MDI)
Gini Impurity of a Node (Slide 264):
\( GI(\tau) = 1 - \sum_{c} p_c^2 \)
Weighted Gini Impurity Reduction (MDI Split):
\( \Delta GI(\tau) = GI(\tau) - \frac{N_{\tau_L}}{N_\tau} GI(\tau_L) - \frac{N_{\tau_R}}{N_\tau} GI(\tau_R) \)
Feature Importance is the weighted impurity decrease averaged across all \( M \) trees:
\( \text{Importance}(X_k) = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{t=1}^M \sum_{\tau \in T_t \text{ split by } X_k} \frac{N_\tau}{N} \Delta GI(\tau) \)
Walkthrough: Gini split reduction
Suppose a dataset has total size \( N = 152 \). A node \( \tau \) with \( N_\tau = 100 \) is split using Inactivity (\( X_5 \)):
• Parent Node Gini: \( GI(\tau) = 0.50 \).
• Left Child (\( N_L = 60 \)): \( GI(\tau_L) = 0.35 \).
• Right Child (\( N_R = 40 \)): \( GI(\tau_R) = 0.20 \).
Impurity Reduction calculation:
\( \Delta GI(\tau) = 0.50 - \frac{60}{100} (0.35) - \frac{40}{100} (0.20) = 0.21 \)
Weighted split contribution to feature importance:
\( \frac{N_\tau}{N} \Delta GI(\tau) = \frac{100}{152} \times 0.21 \approx 0.138 \).
This decrease is summed across all nodes and trees where \( X_5 \) is selected to compute the final feature importance (Economy: 42%, Inactivity: 2%).

📊 Slide 9: Model Selection & Adjusted R-squared Math (LinearRegression+LogisticRegression: Slide 183-188)
Model Selection Criteria
Degree of Freedom (DoF) Formula (Slide 183):
\( \text{DoF} = n - p - 1 \)
where \( n \) is the number of observations and \( p \) is the number of predictors.
Adjusted R-squared (Slide 184):
\( R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1 - R^2) \frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1} \)
Adjusted \( R^2 \) penalises the inclusion of unnecessary variables, preventing overfitting and providing a fairer comparison between models of different complexities (Slide 186).
Performance Metrics & Walkthrough
Standard Regression Error Metrics (Slide 120):
• MSE: \( \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \) (penalises larger errors heavily)
• MAE: \( \text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum |y_i - \hat{y}_i| \) (linear sensitivity)
• RMSE: \( \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{MSE}} \) (preserves original target unit)
Walkthrough: Adjusted R-squared Selection (Slide 188)
Compare two regression models on a dataset of size \( n = 100 \):
• Model A (Baseline, \( p = 8 \) features): achieves \( R^2 = 0.7500 \).
\( R^2_{\text{adj, A}} = 1 - (1 - 0.75) \times \frac{100 - 1}{100 - 8 - 1} \approx 0.7280 \)
• Model B (Ablated, \( p = 5 \) features): achieves \( R^2 = 0.7450 \) (slightly lower raw R²).
\( R^2_{\text{adj, B}} = 1 - (1 - 0.745) \times \frac{100 - 1}{100 - 5 - 1} \approx 0.7314 \)
Conclusion: Model B is preferred since it achieves a higher Adjusted R-squared (\(0.7314 > 0.7280\)) with fewer variables, proving the ablated variables were redundant.

🖥️ Slide 10: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Derivation & Calculation (LinearRegression+LogisticRegression: Slide 168-170)
OLS Mathematical Derivation
Minimize Sum of Squared Errors: \( J(w_0, w_1) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - (w_0 + w_1 x_i))^2 \)
Take partial derivatives and set to zero (Slide 168):
Take \( \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_0} = 0 \implies n w_0 + w_1 \sum x_i = \sum y_i \)
Take \( \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_1} = 0 \implies w_0 \sum x_i + w_1 \sum x_i^2 = \sum x_i y_i \)
Solving the OLS system of normal equations yields:
\( w_1 = \frac{n \sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i}{n \sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2} \)
\( w_0 = \bar{y} - w_1 \bar{x} = \frac{\sum y_i \sum x_i^2 - \sum x_i \sum x_i y_i}{n \sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2} \)
Exam Walkthrough & Error Metrics
Dataset (Glucose vs. Age, \(n=6\)):
• \( \sum A = 247, \quad \sum G = 486 \)
• \( \sum A^2 = 11409, \quad \sum A \cdot G = 20485 \)
Slope (\(w_1\)) and Intercept (\(w_0\)) OLS calculations:
\( w_1 = \frac{6(20485) - 247(486)}{6(11409) - 247^2} = \frac{2868}{7445} \approx 0.39 \)
\( w_0 = \frac{486(11409) - 247(20485)}{7445} \approx 65.14 \)
Model: \( G = 65.14 + 0.39 \cdot A \).
Error Metrics Walkthrough (Slide 178-179):
• Total Sum of Squares: \( SST = \sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2 = 656.00 \)
• Regression Sum of Squares: \( SSR = \sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2 = 188.96 \)
• Error Sum of Squares: \( SSE = \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = 472.12 \)
• Verification: \( SST = SSR + SSE \) analytically (minor difference of 661.08 vs 656.00 in hand-calculated sums is due to rounding in intermediatepredicted values).
R-squared: \( R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SST} = \frac{188.96}{656.00} \approx 0.288 \)

🖥️ Slide 11: Decision Trees, Gini Impurity & Ensemble Principles (Lecture-Five: Slide 264-282, 318)
Decision Tree Splitting Math
Entropy (ID3) (Slide 278): \( H(D) = -\sum p_i \log_2 p_i \)
Gini Impurity (CART) (Slide 264): \( GI(D) = 1 - \sum p_i^2 \)
Weighted Split Gini:
\( GI_{\text{split}} = \sum_{v \in \text{values}} \frac{|D_v|}{|D|} GI(D_v) \)
Bootstrapping Rule (Slide 318): Sampling with replacement yields a distinct representation rate of:
\( 1 - e^{-1} \approx 63.2\% \text{ unique samples, } 36.8\% \text{ duplicates} \)
Exam Walkthrough & Variance Reduction
Gini Calculation (Slide 273): Root Node (n=13, yes=7, no=6):
\( GI(Root) = 1 - \left(\frac{7}{13}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{6}{13}\right)^2 \approx 0.497 \).
Variance Reduction (Regression Trees):
For numerical targets, nodes are split to maximize variance reduction:
• Node Variance: \( \text{Var}(D) = \frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{i \in D} (y_i - \bar{y})^2 \)
• Split Variance: \( \text{Var}_{\text{split}} = \sum \frac{|D_v|}{|D|} \text{Var}(D_v) \)
• Reduction: \( \Delta \text{Var} = \text{Var}(Parent) - \text{Var}_{\text{split}} \)

🖥️ Slide 12: K-Means Clustering & PCA Mathematical Principles (Lecture-Six: Slide 339-342 | Lecture-Seven: Slide 408-413)
K-Means & PCA Formulations
K-Means Centroid Update (Slide 339): Centroids are updated to the mean coordinates of all assigned points:
\( c_k = \frac{1}{|C_k|} \sum_{x_i \in C_k} x_i \)
PCA Covariance Matrix (\( \Sigma \)) (Slide 410):
\( \Sigma = \frac{1}{n-1} X_c^T X_c \)
Characteristic Equation for Eigenvalues (Slide 411):
\( \det(\Sigma - \lambda I) = 0 \)
Principal Component Projection Score (Slide 412):
\( Z = X_c \cdot U \)
K-Means Optimal K-Value Selection (Elbow vs. Silhouette)
1. Elbow Method (Inertia/WCSS) (Slide 341):
We plot Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) to find the "elbow" point where adding more clusters yields diminishing returns in variance explained:
\( \text{WCSS}(K) = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{x_i \in C_k} ||x_i - c_k||^2 \)
In our analysis (Slide 12 chart), WCSS drops sharply at \( K=2 \) and continues to a distinct "elbow" bend at \( K=3 \) before flattening.

2. Silhouette Coefficient (Slide 342):
Evaluates cluster separation. For each sample \( i \):
\( s_i = \frac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i, b_i)} \)
where \( a_i \) is mean intra-cluster distance, and \( b_i \) is mean nearest-cluster distance. The global score is \( \bar{s} = \frac{1}{n}\sum s_i \).
- \( K=2 \) yields \( \bar{s} = 0.377 \) (mathematically optimal).
- \( K=3 \) yields \( \bar{s} = 0.342 \) (slight mathematical drop, but still strong).

3. Why we chose K=3 (Domain Interpretation):
While \( K=2 \) is mathematically optimal, it divides the world binarily (e.g. Developed vs. Developing). This binary split **masks the transition tier of mid-income countries** (like Latin America/Southeast Asia) where sedentary behavior is rising but happiness is not yet matching high-income nations. Selecting \( K=3 \) captures this distinct 3-tier developmental gradient, maximizing the **societal interpretability** of our unsupervised clustering.

Elbow & Silhouette Analysis Curves:
Exam Walkthrough: PCA Calculations
Covariance Matrix: \( \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 4.4 & 5.6 \\ 5.6 & 8.0 \end{bmatrix} \).
Solve characteristic equation:
\( \det \begin{bmatrix} 4.4-\lambda & 5.6 \\ 5.6 & 8.0-\lambda \end{bmatrix} = 0 \)
\( (4.4-\lambda)(8.0-\lambda) - 5.6^2 = 0 \implies \lambda^2 - 12.4\lambda + 3.84 = 0 \)
By quadratic formula:
\( \lambda_1 = 12.08 \quad (\text{PC1, } 97.4\% \text{ variance}) \)
\( \lambda_2 = 0.32 \quad (\text{PC2, } 2.6\% \text{ variance}) \).
Normalized Eigenvector for \( \lambda_1 \):
\( (\Sigma - 12.08 I)\mathbf{v} = 0 \implies -7.68x + 5.6y = 0 \implies \mathbf{u}_1 \approx \begin{bmatrix} 0.59 \\ 0.81 \end{bmatrix} \).
Projection score of centered point \( [3, 4] \):
\( PC_1 = 3 \cdot 0.59 + 4 \cdot 0.81 = 5.0 \).
Causal DAG: Why Inactivity is a Spurious Correlation
Using Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) and backdoor adjustment to resolve confounding bias.
Causal DAG: Resolving the Spurious Paradox
📐 What is a DAG? A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) uses arrows (→) to map causal assumptions. It helps identify if a statistical correlation is real or just a confounding illusion.
⛓️ Confounding & Backdoor Path: GDP acts as a confounder: it causes Happiness (wealth) and Inactivity (desk jobs). This opens a backdoor path (Inactivity ← GDP → Happiness), creating a fake positive correlation.
❌ Why the direct coefficient "Collapsed" to +0.0017:
In OLS, we control for GDP to block the backdoor path. Once blocked, the spurious link vanishes: the inactivity coefficient collapses from +0.0406 → +0.0017 (P = 0.727, Insignificant).
💡 Policy Implications:
While active lifestyles are vital for physical health (mitigating NCDs), physical inactivity has no direct or indirect impact on national happiness when controlling for wealth. Interventions aiming to raise well-being should focus on economic security and social support.

🤖 Slide 13: Cooperative Game Theory & Causal Inference (Advanced ML Interpretability)
Shapley Value Formulation
Shapley Value (SHAP) Formula:
\( \phi_i(x) = \sum_{S \subseteq F \setminus \{i\}} \frac{|S|!(|F| - |S| - 1)!}{|F|!} [f_x(S \cup \{i\}) - f_x(S)] \)
where \( F \) is the total feature set, \( S \) is a subset of features excluding feature \( i \), and \( f_x(S) \) is the prediction of model using only subset \( S \).
Causal Backdoor Adjustment: To estimate the true effect of Inactivity (\(X\)) on Happiness (\(Y\)), we block all backdoor paths by conditioning on the d-separating set \( W = \{\text{Log GDP}, \text{Social}, \text{Health}\} \):
\( P(Y | do(X)) = \sum_w P(Y | X, w) P(w) \)
SHAP Axioms
• Local Accuracy (Efficiency): The sum of SHAP values equals the difference between model output and base value: \( \sum \phi_i(x) = f(x) - \mathbb{E}[f(X)] \).
• Missingness: A feature with no impact has zero contribution: \( x_i = 0 \implies \phi_i(x) = 0 \).
• Consistency: If a model changes so that feature \( i \)'s marginal contribution increases, its SHAP value must increase.
Macro-Policy Optimization: How is National Happiness Generated?
Balancing baseline national foundations with model-derived marginal slopes to maximize well-being ROI.
🏆 Scientific Findings: 5 Steps to Causal Clarity
1. EDA & Feature Engineering Discovered a paradox (r = +0.40) where inactivity seemingly boosted happiness, then reduced 27 raw parameters to 5 core features.
2. Linear & Multiple Regression Controlling for socioeconomics caused the inactivity coefficient to collapse to ≈0 (P=0.727), resolving the paradox mathematically.
3. Non-Linear Random Forest Confirmed GDP and Health dominate the variance (basic foundation), while inactivity accounts for merely ~2% of global importance.
4. Unsupervised K-Means Grouped the world into 3 distinct economic tiers, proving sedentary habits align with wealthy urbanization, not happiness.
5. Causal DAG Analysis Causal mapping structurally proved GDP is the ultimate confounder driving both higher happiness and higher inactivity simultaneously.

Well-Being ROI: Balancing Baseline & Slope

Estimating shifts from a Uniform 10% Improvement policy (Global Happiness Baseline = 5.37):

  • 🕊️ Freedom +10% (Mean=0.43, β=2.04) +0.09 (to 5.46)
  • 💚 Health +10% (Mean=0.63, β=1.46) +0.09 (to 5.46)
  • 👨‍👩‍👧 Family +10% (Mean=0.99, β=1.13) +0.11 (to 5.48)
  • 📈 GDP +10% (Mean=0.84, β=0.56) +0.05 (to 5.42)
  • 🚶‍♂️ Inactivity -10% (Mean=28.6%, β≈0.00) -0.00 (stat. zero)
💡 Policy Balancing Act: Optimal policy returns depend on both the Current Baseline Status (Principal) and the Marginal Slope (Efficiency/β). While Freedom has a steep slope (β=2.04), its low global baseline (0.43) yields a similar absolute happiness gain (+0.09) to Health, which has a higher baseline (0.63) but a flatter slope (β=1.46). Policy simulations balance these two dimensions to calculate the final absolute gains.

*Conclusion: Causal analysis indicates that reducing adult inactivity will yield statistically zero direct gains in happiness.

Bias-Variance & Stratification Math
Bias-Variance Loss Decomposition (Slide 415): Expected test loss decomposes into:
\( \mathbb{E}[L] = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 \)
where:
• \( \text{Bias}[\hat{f}(x)] = \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)] - f(x) \) (systematic error)
• \( \text{Var}[\hat{f}(x)] = \mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)])^2] \) (model sensitivity)
• \( \sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 \) (irreducible error / noise variance)
Stratified K-Fold Class Proportions (Slide 223):
\( \frac{n_{jk}}{n_j} \approx \frac{N_k}{N} \)
Exam Walkthrough: Stratified Folds
Suppose a dataset has total samples \( N = 1000 \). Class Male has \( N_M = 600 \) (60%), and Class Female has \( N_F = 400 \) (40%).

Applying a Stratified 5-Fold Split (\( K = 5 \)):
• Each fold size is \( n_j = 1000 / 5 = 200 \) samples.
• To preserve class proportions, each fold is allocated exactly:
Male: \( 200 \times 60\% = 120 \) samples
Female: \( 200 \times 40\% = 80 \) samples
This preserves class proportions perfectly across all 5 validation folds (Slide 225).

🖥️ Slide 15: Simulator Math & ML Advisor Logic (Real-Time Counterfactual Calculations)
Real-Time Prediction Formulation
1. Real-Time Counterfactual Prediction Score:
Predicted happiness \( \hat{Y}_{\text{sim}} \) is calculated using a local Taylor expansion centered at the country's actual baseline happiness \( Y_{\text{baseline}} \) with local slopes \( w_{c, j} \):
\( \hat{Y}_{\text{sim}} = Y_{\text{baseline}} + \sum_{j=1}^5 w_{c, j} (x'_j - x_{c, j}) \)
where at baseline (when user adjustments are zero), the projected score matches the actual country baseline score exactly.
2. Dynamic Slope approximation via local SHAP derivatives:
We use the selected country's local SHAP value \( \phi_{c, j} \) to approximate the local derivative at the country's baseline raw value \( x_{c, j} \):
\( w_{c, j} = \frac{\phi_{c, j}}{x_{c, j} - \bar{x}_j} \quad \text{for } |x_{c, j} - \bar{x}_j| \ge 0.05 \)
where \( \bar{x}_j \) is the global mean. If the difference is \( < 0.05 \), we fall back to the global coefficient \( w_{c, j} = w_{\text{global}, j} \).
UI Interface to Mathematical Parameters Mapping
• Country Dropdown: Selects country \( c \), loading its baseline raw vector \( \mathbf{x}_c = [x_{c, 1}, \dots, x_{c, 5}] \) and local SHAP vector \( \mathbf{\phi}_c \).
• Left Sliders (Inputs): Adjusts slider \( j \) to counterfactual value \( x'_j \), determining the delta change: \( \Delta x_j = x'_j - x_{c, j} \).
• Predicted Happiness (Output): Instantly calculates and displays: \( Y_{\text{baseline}} + \sum w_{c, j} \Delta x_j \).
• Policy Recommendation Tags: Priority tags are mapped to local slope leverage \( w_{c, j} \) and baseline relative coordinate \( x_{c, j} - \bar{x}_j \).
Machine Learning Model Bindings & Closed-Loop Integration
This interactive simulator directly applies the parameters and mathematical structures trained during the project's machine learning phase: • Multiple Linear Regression (Slide 10): Powers the global base model. OLS intercept (\( w_0 = 2.0030 \)) and global feature coefficients (\( \mathbf{w}_{\text{global}} \)) serve as the fallbacks for the advisor.
• Random Forest & Gradient Boosting SHAP values (Slide 13): Supplies the local feature contributions (\( \mathbf{\phi}_c \)) for each country. By dividing the SHAP value by the deviation from the mean, we extract the **localized marginal impact rate** (local slope) tailored to each nation's current development stage.
• Statistical Control Override: Multiple regression proved that Physical Inactivity's coefficient collapses to near zero (\( \beta \approx 0.00 \), \( p = 0.94 \)) when controlling for GDP. The advisor applies this ML insight by classifying inactivity as "Low Leverage" and bypassing counterfactual updates for it.
• Policy Optimization: The advisor prioritizes policy recommendation tags based on the ratio of baseline features to the maximum dataset value and the magnitude of the SHAP-derived local slope (\( w_{c, j} \)), guiding users toward high-leverage reforms.
Safeguards & Advisor Rules
3. Heuristic Rules & Safeguards:
• Diminishing Returns: Negative slopes for positive drivers are capped: \( w_{c, j} = 0.2 \cdot w_{\text{global}, j} \).
• Outlier Cap: Capped at three times global weight: \( w_{c, j} = \min(w_{c, j}, 3 \cdot w_{\text{global}, j}) \).
• Fix First: Raw value below mean \( (x_{c, j} < \bar{x}_j) \) AND local slope \( w_{c, j} \) is high.
• Improve Next: Raw value near mean or moderate slope leverage.
• Low Leverage: Specifically assigned to Physical Inactivity (\( \beta \approx 0.00 \)).
Walkthrough: Live Simulation Mechanics (Germany)
• Step 1: Load Country Baseline (Set Reference Vector)
Selecting Germany (\( c \)) loads its historical baseline values:
- Baseline Happiness Score (\( Y_{\text{baseline}} \)) = 6.95
- Raw GDP per Capita (\( x_{c, 1} \)) = 1.33 (versus the global average GDP \( \bar{x}_1 = 0.84 \))
- GDP SHAP Contribution (\( \phi_{c, 1} \)) = +0.69 (measures how much Germany's GDP contributes to its happiness above the global baseline)

• Step 2: Compute Local Slope (Marginal Coefficient)
We approximate the local derivative/slope (\( w_{c, 1} \)) for GDP using its SHAP contribution divided by its deviation from the global mean:
\( w_{c, 1} = \frac{\phi_{c, 1}}{x_{c, 1} - \bar{x}_1} = \frac{+0.69}{1.33 - 0.84} = 1.41 \)
Interpretation: In Germany's local context, for every 1.0 unit increase in GDP per capita, national happiness score is expected to increase by +1.41.

• Step 3: User Adjusts Slider (Policy Scenario Change)
The user raises Germany's GDP slider by +0.10 to a new counterfactual value \( x'_1 = 1.43 \):
- Delta Change (\( \Delta x_1 \)) = \( x'_1 - x_{c, 1} = 1.43 - 1.33 = +0.10 \)

• Step 4: Compute Policy Impact
The counterfactual change in happiness resulting from the GDP policy adjustment is:
\( \text{Impact}_1 = w_{c, 1} \cdot \Delta x_1 = 1.41 \times (+0.10) = +0.141 \)

• Step 5: Update Projected Happiness Score
The simulator calculates the new score (\( \hat{Y}_{\text{sim}} \)) by adding the policy impact to the historical baseline score:
\( \hat{Y}_{\text{sim}} = Y_{\text{baseline}} + \text{Impact}_1 = 6.95 + 0.141 = 7.091 \approx 7.09 \)
The UI displays a Projected Score of 7.09, and Net Happiness Impact shows +0.14!
